title: By night, from mosque to mosque
hook: glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (17:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabr, the patience An-Nahl ends on, commanded and given at once. Today, a new surah.

Surah seventeen opens with a whole night, and tells it in a single verse. No buildup, no description of the road. Just a sentence of praise, and inside it, a journey. The surah is named for that night: Al-Isra, the Night Journey. Its other name is Bani Isra'il, the Children of Israel. Some Muslims mark the night each year in the month of Rajab, though its date is debated.

In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship". The verse goes on: whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We might show him some of Our signs. Start with the first word, subhana: glory be, far above any fault. The verse opens with praise of the One who did the carrying, not the one who was carried. And notice what he's called. Not prophet, not messenger. 'Abd: servant. On that night, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is named by a humble title. Then the two places. The Sacred Mosque is in Mecca, around the Ka'bah. The Farthest Mosque, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, is understood by Muslims as Jerusalem. Masjid literally means a place of prostration. The hadith collections fill in what the verse leaves out. In Bukhari and Muslim, a white mount named Buraq carries him; in Muslim's collection he leads the earlier prophets in prayer in Jerusalem; then comes the Mi'raj, the ascent through the heavens, where the five daily prayers are given. Scholars have discussed the nature of the journey from early on. Commentators such as at-Tabari held it was in body and spirit; some early reports describe it as a vision. Some biographies place it in a hard season, after the Prophet had lost his wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib, when doors in Mecca and Ta'if were closing; its date is debated. Read that way, the night comes in the middle of loss: not carried away from trouble, but shown signs in the middle of it.
screen: `SUBHANA: GLORY TO THE ONE WHO CARRIED.` · `'ABD: A HUMBLE TITLE.` · `MECCA TO JERUSALEM, THEN THE ASCENT.` · `AFTER A YEAR OF LOSS, SOME SAY.` · then, large: `BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look at the night sky if it's dark, or through a window, or close your eyes and remember the last clear night you saw, and notice how far away the farthest light is. Let yourself feel small under it, not in a bad way. If you pray, say subhan Allah, glory to God, once, quietly.
By night. The Isra: a servant carried from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, in the dark, to be shown signs. Today's word.
Your line: taken by night. Some signs only show up in the dark. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Muslims mark Laylat al-Isra wal-Mi'raj, commonly on 27 Rajab, with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and talks retelling the journey; practice varies, and some scholars caution against fixing special rites to the date.

fork.setup: you've lost your wife and your uncle in the same season, and doors are closing around you. what does the night bring, as some biographies tell it?
options: a sign that it's time to give up.
a journey by night, and signs shown to him.

fork.reveal: he is carried by night from Mecca to Jerusalem and shown signs, in the middle of a hard season, as those biographies tell it, not after it.

original.note: Arabic: He carried His servant by night (17:1). Isra, the night journey, comes from this verb.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a miraculous trip.
what it means: the verse praises God, calls Muhammad a servant, and sets the journey from Mecca to Jerusalem in one sentence.
what a scholar hears: asra already means to travel by night, yet the verse adds laylan, by night; commentators say it stresses a part of a single night.
recall: wisdom: knowing when to pull back

chat.says: What's the Night Journey that Surah seventeen begins with?
options: God carried His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.
The Prophet's move from Mecca to Medina to escape those plotting against him.
The night the Qur'an was first revealed, in a cave outside of Mecca.

Editor review (y2 444–462): cut superlatives ('one of the most talked-about nights', 'the greatest night of his life', 'the humblest title') and the unsourced 27 Rajab date and 'many Muslims' from the spoken script. Leading the prophets in prayer was credited to Bukhari and Muslim; it is now credited to Muslim only. 'Most hold body and spirit' is now attributed (at-Tabari). The setting after Khadijah and Abu Talib was stated as fact; sirah sources differ on the date (Ibn Ishaq's order does not clearly put it after), so it now says 'some biographies' and the source line changed.
